⑤ How Much Sharing Prevents It?
The horizontal axis is the redistribution rate, the vertical axis is the Gini coefficient at the end. Each dot is one run.

What it shows: Even when every trade is fair, in a structure where chance compounds, wealth concentrates in a few hands over time. Once someone becomes poor, the amount they can bet is small, so recovery is slow. And even a small amount of redistribution reduces the concentration greatly.

What it doesn't show: Real wealth comes from work, inheritance, investment and institutions, and this model has no production. The redistribution rate is a "share collected per round" and can't be compared directly with real tax rates, nor does it say which policy is right. The assumption that trades are truly fair also differs from reality.

This model is a variant of the exchange model known in econophysics as the "yard-sale model." The key points are that the stake is based on the poorer person's wealth and that there is a redistribution term. It does not reproduce the numbers of a specific paper; it is this project's own implementation.
1,000 people, with 1,000 trades per round (random pairs). Total wealth is always constant at 1,000 (verify with node tools/validate-wealth.js).

Why Do Only the Top 1% of YouTubers Break Through? · Simulatio Lab
Does good content win, or does whoever broke out first? See how subscribers concentrate when recommendations follow popularity.

Do well-made videos take off, or do channels that took off first keep taking off? Run a subscriber race among 200 channels, and compare "parallel universes" that differ only by chance under the same conditions.
Each channel has a fixed content quality. The closer to blue, the higher the quality; the closer to red, the lower.
Each round, 100 viewers arrive and each subscribes to one channel.
Viewers follow popularity-based recommendations some of the time. The more popular a channel, the more it is recommended, so channels with more subscribers grow faster.
The remaining viewers choose in proportion to quality. Pressing "Same settings, new luck" opens a parallel universe with the same set of channels but different chance.

The top 12 channels by subscribers. Bar color is quality, and the quality rank is written under each name.

③ Eight Parallel Universes
Starting from the same channels and varying only chance across 8 runs, this shows the quality rank of the channel that came out #1.
④ As Popularity-Based Recommendation Grows

The horizontal axis is the share of popularity-based recommendations. The blue line is the correlation between quality and outcome (1 means outcomes follow quality), and the gold line is the share of subscriptions taken by the top 10% of channels.

What it shows: The larger the share of popularity-based recommendations, the more subscriptions concentrate in a few channels and the weaker the link between quality and outcome becomes. Even starting from the same channels, who ends up #1 can be completely different by chance, so there is no guarantee that today's #1 is the best channel.

What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean quality is useless. When popularity-based recommendation is weak, outcomes follow quality. Real YouTube recommendations and viewer behavior are far more complex, and this model has no video topics, upload frequency or unsubscribes. The degree of the algorithm's popularity bias (recommending the larger of 2 candidates) is also this project's assumption.

A model inspired by preferential attachment (the "rich get richer" idea in the Barabási–Albert family) and by the experiment of Salganik, Dodds, Watts (2006), Science 311, on how social influence makes the success of music unpredictable. It does not reproduce a paper's numbers; it is this project's own design.

Popularity-based recommendation draws 2 candidates in proportion to subscribers+1 and recommends the larger. Drawing only 1 gives weak concentration (the top 10% hold about 23–33%), so we assumed the algorithm leans further toward popularity.
Quality is log-normal (σ=0.5) generated from a fixed seed, so the parallel universes share the same set of channels. You can verify with node tools/validate-more.js youtube.
The code is available on GitHub.
Why Are a Few Words Used Constantly? · Simulatio Lab
In books and newspapers alike, a handful of words make up most of the text. See for yourself whether "copying earlier words" alone creates this pile-up.

A few words like "the", "of" and "and" make up a large part of any text, while most words almost never appear. Can this pile-up be produced not by what the words mean, but only by the habit of reusing what was already written?

The text is written one word at a time. With a small probability (the new-word probability) a brand-new word is invented; otherwise a word that already appeared is used again. The words are meaningless made-up ones (kia, marthiro, and so on).
